stages.title: The Screenplay Page
stages.description: How a film script is laid out so a reader, and later a crew, can see the scene: sluglines, action, character cues and dialogue.
learningObjectives: Name the main elements of a screenplay page
Write a scene heading that states interior or exterior, place and time
Keep action to what can be seen or heard, written in the present tense
Distinguish a spec script from a shooting script

explainBack.question: You are formatting the opening of a short film: two people argue in a kitchen at night, then one steps outside. Describe the elements you would put on the page, and how a spec script differs from a shooting script.
rubric: A slugline starts each scene and states INT. or EXT., the location and the time of day; stepping outside begins a new scene
Action is written in the present tense and is limited to what the audience can see or hear
Dialogue is the words the characters speak, set apart from the action
One page is only a rough estimate of one minute, and the standard type is 12-point Courier
A spec script is written to be sold with no upfront payment; a shooting script is where the sluglines are numbered

resources.title: Anatomy of a Screenplay — Movie Script Format Explained (And Why It Matters)
resources.description: StudioBinder walks through the six basic screenplay elements, starting with the slugline, action and character cues.
keyPoints: A slugline holds location and time: EXT. outside, INT. inside, INT./EXT. when both
Keep a scene heading to one line; time can be DAY, NIGHT, CONTINUOUS or MOMENTS LATER
Action is what is seen or heard; a character name is uppercase before dialogue
Extensions such as voice-over and off-screen sit with the character name

resources.title: Medium and Format
resources.description: BBC Writers explains why film, television and radio each have a format, and what a single film script is expected to be.
keyPoints: Formats exist because of the medium: a correct layout helps a reader and the later rewrite
A single film is a complete story, usually 75 to 120 minutes, sent as a full script
TV series, serials and singles are different submissions: a series needs a pilot plus a short outline of later episodes
Produced BBC scripts in the Script Library show the formats in use

resources.title: Screenplay
resources.description: What a screenplay contains, why one page is treated as about a minute, and how a spec script differs from a shooting script.
keyPoints: A screenplay describes movement, action, expression and dialogue in a set format
One page is a rough estimate of one minute of screen time, and the standard font is 12-point Courier
Action is written in the present tense and limited to what can be seen or heard; dialogue is the spoken words
A slugline starts each scene with INT. or EXT., the location and the time of day
A spec script is written to sell with no upfront payment; a shooting script numbers the sluglines

resources.title: Scene Headings (Sluglines)
resources.description: What a slugline tells a reader and a crew: interior or exterior, where, and when.
keyPoints: A scene heading is one line in capitals: INT. or EXT., location, then time of day
INT. is indoors and EXT. is outdoors; the split matters for light, sound and location
DAY and NIGHT are the common times and tell the reader how the light should feel
A heading without INT. or EXT. is a secondary heading, not a new primary scene

stages.title: Three-Act Structure
stages.description: Setup, confrontation and resolution: the inciting incident, the turn into act two, and the climax that answers the dramatic question.
learningObjectives: Name the three acts and what each one is for
Define the inciting incident and the first plot point
Explain why act two raises the stakes before the protagonist can resolve them
State what the climax answers

explainBack.question: Outline a feature in three acts. Where do the inciting incident and the first plot point sit, what happens to the protagonist in the middle, and what must the climax settle?
rubric: Syd Field named the three acts Setup, Confrontation and Resolution in Screenplay (1979)
Act one establishes characters, relationships and the world, then an inciting incident confronts the protagonist
The first plot point ends act one, changes the protagonist's life and raises a dramatic question
Act two is rising action: attempts to solve the problem get worse until the protagonist changes
The climax brings the main tension to its peak and answers the dramatic question

resources.title: THREE ACT STORY STRUCTURE EXAMPLES - Story Structure For Film - Juno - Filmmaking 101
resources.description: A film-by-film walkthrough of setup, confrontation and resolution, using Juno as the example.
keyPoints: Act one is the setup, act two the confrontation, act three the resolution
The inciting incident confronts the main character; their decision leads into act two
Act two is rising action and is where a character arc can take hold
The climax is the most dramatic scene, and it answers the question the inciting incident raised

resources.title: Three-act structure
resources.description: The encyclopedia account of setup, confrontation and resolution, including Field's terms and the dramatic question.
keyPoints: The three acts are often called the Setup, the Confrontation and the Resolution
Syd Field described the model in his 1979 book Screenplay
The inciting incident leads to a first plot point that ends act one and raises a dramatic question
Act two is rising action; the protagonist lacks the skill to win until they change
The climax answers the dramatic question

resources.title: Three Act Structure in Film: Definition and Examples
resources.description: StudioBinder's account of beginning, middle and end, with Field's Setup, Confrontation and Resolution.
keyPoints: Act one sets up the world, the goal and the obstacles, often the first 20 to 30 minutes
The inciting incident kickstarts the story
Act two raises the stakes and often leads to the worst thing that can happen
Act three resolves the goal, whether the ending is happy or sad

stages.title: Character Change
stages.description: How a protagonist starts as one kind of person and is forced to change because they cannot yet overcome the opposition.
learningObjectives: Define a character arc
Explain why the protagonist often cannot win at the start
Place the arc against the three acts
Tell a change of self-awareness from a change of skill

explainBack.question: A protagonist begins the film unable to deal with the problem. Describe what a character arc is, how it moves through the three acts, and what kind of change the climax is for.
rubric: A character arc is the inner change across the story: the person begins as one sort of person and becomes another
They often cannot overcome the opposition yet because they lack skill, knowledge, resources or allies
Act one establishes the arc; the inciting incident and first turning point make life unable to stay the same
Act two is where they learn skills and, sometimes late, raise their self-awareness
At the climax the dramatic question is answered and the emphasis shifts to who they are becoming

resources.title: Character arc
resources.description: How a lead character transforms across a story, set beside the three-act narrative.
keyPoints: A character arc is the transformation of a character over the story
Lead characters are the ones most likely to arc, though lesser characters can change too
The protagonist often cannot win at first and must learn, or find a mentor, to go on
Act two develops the arc through worsening situations; the climax gives a new sense of who they are becoming
In episodic television an arc can run past a single episode and keep viewers returning

resources.title: Screenplay Primers
resources.description: Short craft notes from the Writers Guild Foundation library, including the note that every character sounds the same.
keyPoints: The primers cover formatting and craft with examples from produced scripts
They answer notes such as bigger stakes and characters who all sound the same
Getting a reader to invest takes on-page craft, not only the idea
They are meant as a quick lesson when there is no time to read a full screenplay

stages.title: Scenes and Action
stages.description: How a scene heading starts a unit of drama, and how action lines stay on what the camera can record.
learningObjectives: Read a BBC film scene heading and the action under it
Limit an action paragraph and say why
Keep thoughts and back-story out of the action
Say what a spec film script omits that a shooting script includes

explainBack.question: Rewrite the idea 'she remembers her father and feels afraid' as a screenplay scene. What goes in the heading, what goes in the action, and what does not belong on a spec page?
rubric: A scene heading is in capitals and states interior or exterior, the location, and day or night
Action deals only with what is happening on the screen and must not narrate thoughts or back-story
An action paragraph is kept to about four or five lines, each paragraph a beat
A new scene is separated from the last, and a heading is followed by a line of action
Scene numbers and camera directions belong on a shooting script, not a spec film script

resources.title: Screenplay format
resources.description: The BBC Writersroom sample of film screenplay format, from the opening FADE IN through action and the end of a spec script.
keyPoints: Scene headings are in capitals and state interior or exterior, location, and day or night
Action is what is happening on screen and must not stray into thoughts or back-story
Limit an action paragraph to four or five lines; treat each paragraph as a beat
Scene numbers and camera directions are for shooting scripts, not a spec film script
A film script signs off with FADE OUT. and THE END; page one is the first scene, not the title page

resources.title: Understanding screenplay elements
resources.description: StudioBinder's support note on scene headings, action, character, extensions and parentheticals.
keyPoints: A scene heading is INT or EXT, location, and time of day
Action sits under the heading and describes what will be seen or heard
Extensions such as V.O. and O.S. sit next to the character name
A parenthetical under the name is a note on how the line is performed

resources.title: Screenplay format for TV shows
resources.description: How a filmed television script marks a teaser and acts, and how that differs from an unbroken feature.
keyPoints: Teasers and acts begin with FADE IN: and a scene heading
Action still describes only the screen, in short paragraphs
FADE OUT. appears at the end of an act and at the end of the script
Page one begins with the teaser, not the title page

stages.title: Dialogue and Subtext
stages.description: Spoken lines that do more than one job, and the meaning that stays under the words.
learningObjectives: Define subtext
Give a line more than one job
Use a parenthetical only when the line needs it
Show unspoken meaning in action and in what is not said

explainBack.question: Two characters talk about the weather while one is about to deliver bad news. Explain what subtext is, how the spoken line should earn its place, and where a parenthetical helps or gets in the way.
rubric: Subtext is meaning that is not stated and must be inferred; a meaning said outright is not subtext
Dialogue that states exactly what the character means is often called on the nose and flattens tension
A line should advance the plot, reveal character, or create conflict
A parenthetical is a short direction between the cue and the line; film can show what a play would have to say
Body language, a leading question, or a too-quiet answer can carry the unspoken meaning

resources.title: Writing Subtext  — The Secret to Writing What's Under the Surface
resources.description: StudioBinder on three ways to write the unspoken meaning: in the dialogue, in the action, and in the performance.
keyPoints: Subtext is the unspoken or secondary meaning under what is said and done
The same line changes when the context around it changes
Dialogue can leave the direct threat unsaid, as in an offer he cannot refuse
Action and parentheticals can carry meaning, and the writer should not direct every performance

resources.title: Subtext
resources.description: The underlying meaning an audience infers, including how film puts that meaning in behaviour as well as words.
keyPoints: Subtext is implicit meaning that is understood without being stated
A meaning stated explicitly is not subtext
Writing that says exactly what it means is often called on the nose
Body language, a leading question, or a one-word answer can carry the hidden meaning
Stanislavski developed the idea of unspoken intention beneath dialogue

resources.title: Dialogue and Parentheticals
resources.description: How film dialogue can stay lean because the camera can show what a stage play would have to speak.
keyPoints: Film dialogue can be leaner than stage dialogue because the camera communicates
A line should advance the plot, reveal character, or create conflict
A parenthetical is a brief lowercase note between the character cue and the speech
Subtext is the real subject under a surface conversation the characters can say aloud

stages.title: Fountain, a Plain-Text Script
stages.description: Fountain is a plain-text way to write a formatted screenplay in any editor, merged from two earlier projects.
learningObjectives: Say what Fountain is and what it lets a writer use
Name the two projects it was merged from
Name the writers who joined those projects
Give examples of software that can read it

explainBack.question: A writer wants to draft a screenplay in an ordinary text editor. Explain what Fountain is, where it came from, and why that is enough to produce a formatted script.
rubric: Fountain is a free, open-source plain-text markup language for writing a formatted screenplay in any text editor
The name comes from Fountain Avenue, the Hollywood shortcut
It was inspired by Markdown and merged two projects: Scrippets, by John August and Nima Yousefi, and Screenplay Markdown, by Stu Maschwitz
August and Maschwitz combined those projects into Fountain
Editors and screenwriting apps that implement it include Scrivener, Slugline, Trelby and Vim

resources.title: Fountain (markup language)
resources.description: What Fountain is, the two projects it joined, and the editors that can turn that plain text into a screenplay.
keyPoints: Fountain is a free open-source plain-text markup language for a formatted screenplay in any text editor
The name comes from Fountain Avenue, the Hollywood shortcut
It was inspired by Markdown
It merged Scrippets (John August and Nima Yousefi) with Screenplay Markdown (Stu Maschwitz)
Implementations include Scrivener, Slugline, Trelby, Vim and Visual Studio Code

stages.title: The First Page and What to Send
stages.description: Why the opening page has to earn the next one, and how a submission stays inside a readable length and layout.
learningObjectives: Say what the first page of a feature is expected to do
Give the BBC's page-count window for a submitted script
Name the font they recommend for film and TV
Avoid layout tricks that inflate the page count

explainBack.question: A reader opens your feature. What must page one do, and how would you lay out a BBC submission so the length and the type stay within their guidance?
rubric: Page one has to show what the film is about, show cinematic writing, and make the reader turn the page
Seasoned readers often decide from the first page, even when the old advice allowed ten pages
BBC submissions are 30 to 130 dialogue pages, excluding the title page and other front matter
Film and TV scripts should use Courier 12-point, with ordinary margins
Do not start a new page for every scene, and do not widen the margins to stretch the page count

resources.title: Writing Your Screenplay: Page One
resources.description: The Writers Guild Foundation on why the first page of a feature has to hook a reader.
keyPoints: Reading scripts is treated as essential to becoming a better writer
Page one should say what the movie is about, prove cinematic writing, and compel the next page
The generous advice is ten pages to hook a reader; seasoned readers often decide on page one
The series is about words on the page of a feature draft, not an outline

resources.title: BBC Writers Script Submission Style Guide
resources.description: BBC guidance on length, Courier 12-point, margins and continuous scenes for a script submission.
keyPoints: Submitted scripts must be 30 to 130 pages of dialogue, not counting the title page
There is no single correct format; the guide is a readable default
TV and film scripts should use Courier 12-point
Keep standard margins and do not give each scene its own page
Number the scenes and the pages

resources.title: Resource Center
resources.description: The Foundation's index of free craft and business material, including where to find scripts and which fellowships exist.
keyPoints: The center collects vetted material on the craft and the business of screenwriting
It points to videos, TV format notes, script libraries and writing classes
Fellowship programmes are listed alongside the craft primers
Suggestions for additions go to the Foundation

stages.title: Copyright in the Script
stages.description: What copyright already covers when a script is written, and what marking the pages does and does not change.
learningObjectives: State when UK copyright arises
Name the uses copyright can stop
Say what the copyright symbol changes
Note that protection can extend abroad

explainBack.question: You finish an original short-film script in the UK. Explain what copyright you already have, what other people cannot do with it, and whether registering or printing a © line is what creates the right.
rubric: Copyright is automatic: there is no application, no fee, and no UK register of copyright works
Original dramatic work, which includes a script, is protected when it is created
Other people cannot copy it, share copies, perform or show it in public, adapt it, or put it on the internet without permission
Adding ©, a name and a year does not change how strong the protection is
International agreements such as the Berne Convention can protect the work in other countries

resources.title: How copyright protects your work
resources.description: The UK government overview of automatic copyright in original dramatic work, including what a © mark does not change.
keyPoints: Protection is automatic; you do not apply or pay, and the UK has no copyright register
Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic work is covered when you create it
Others cannot copy, distribute, perform, adapt or upload the work without permission
Marking © with your name and the year does not change the level of protection
The Berne Convention can protect the work in other countries

resources.title: TV Format Fundamentals
resources.description: A Foundation series on how television formats differ in act structure, from single-camera sitcom to serialized drama.
keyPoints: The series looks at the act structure of current and classic television formats
The aim is to notice the conventions of a format and apply them in a spec
Separate posts cover single-camera sitcoms, serialized drama and animated sitcoms
A companion spec-primer series breaks down individual series

name: Screenwriting
description: Learn to write a script someone could shoot: the screenplay page, three-act structure, character change, scenes, dialogue and subtext, plain-text Fountain, and what copyright already covers.
